articles.title: She left school, and now she is the only woman running the sound desk at her church
articles.deck: Esther grew up the eldest of four daughters of daily-wage workers, and was pulled out of English-medium school so a younger sister could stay in. Then the church asked for someone to learn the mixer.

hero.alt: Esther resting her chin on her hand beside a Studiomaster mixing desk in her church

interviewMeta.subject: Esther
interviewMeta.subjectBio: A sound operator on the technical crew of her church, and a tailor. She is identified by first name only.

archiveMeta.editNote: Published as it appeared in the March 2013 issue. Column reading order repaired and typographical errors corrected; the wording is otherwise unchanged. She was identified by first name only in the original and remains so here.

body.v: Esther is a school drop-out student but has the passion to do something for the Lord. She went into depression due to her family and education disturbances. She was looking for some opportunity to get peace in her mind.

As a Christian girl she was attending the youth fellowship meeting in her church and got to know more about Jesus. She tried to forget the present status and seek how she can spend more time for the Lord.

She found interest in sound management and started learning the sound equipment, and later joined the sound crew in her local church. Esther has rediscovered her hidden talent and is using it for the Kingdom.
“I was doing all these things only for my enjoyment”
5Talents: Hello Esther, greetings from 5Talents. How are you?
Hello, I am doing well by the grace of God. Thank you.
5Talents: When and how did you come in faith in Christ Jesus as your personal saviour?

I have been born and brought up in a Christian family and I was living a normal life unlike other Christians. I used to attend Sunday school when I was a child, and gradually as I grew older, I started attending the youth meeting, where I go there to enjoy myself listening to the music and songs.

I have been actively participating in choir singing, performing choreographies and also for interceding prayers. But I did not believe God completely at that time. I was doing all these things only for my enjoyment with friends of mine in church, and to get a good name amongst elders and my parents.
Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, before you were born I set you apart…
body.highlight: before you were born I set you apart

body.v: As the word of God says in Jeremiah 1:5, so He knows me well even though I didn't believe Him.
“Why is this poverty with my family?”

It was one fine day I was in the youth meeting singing songs and worshipping the Lord with a burdened heart. I was worried about my career, as I hail from a middle class family and I have got three younger sisters to look after, as my parents are uneducated and they are daily wage workers. It was hard for my parents to educate four of us in English medium schools, and hence three of us including me studied in a Government Telugu medium. Only my fourth sister was able to get education in an English private school.

In those days, I was in depression, anxiety and with a lot of anger, thinking: why did God allow me to be born in this family? Why is this poverty with my family? These sorts of questions were troubling me and making me depart from the Lord.

God was so gracious and loving to me in spite of my weaknesses. He spoke to me through the same verse, Jer 1:5, while the praise and worship was going on. God's words were clear to my conscience, saying: “I am here for you and I will take care of your career.”

At the end of the worship, I felt all peace and joy in my heart. I forgot about the questions which were troubling me, and I came to know that I was doing wrong till now by questioning God. Soon, I prayed to the Lord to forgive me for my sins and accepted Him as my personal saviour and Lord. Oh, it was the day of my salvation, and I can never forget that night what I have encountered with my Lord Jesus.
“Can I do it?”
5Talents: What are the talents you discovered to use for the kingdom of the Lord?

I was selected for choir singing in my church and also I was in the choreography team for programs carried out in church. I personally know tailoring work and I can stitch designer dresses and blouses effectively. These are a few talents which I have discovered that God has given me to glorify His name and to equip me in the society. Apart from this, I had interest towards the sound operating mixer which was in our church and operated by one of our youth members.

One day, there was an announcement in our church regarding the need of a sound operating technician, and soon my heart overwhelmed with joy, as I also can give my concern that I have interest towards learning the operating of the sound mixer. But I was afraid too, thinking, “Can I do it, as I don't have knowledge regarding the sound operating earlier?”

I prayed to God asking His will in my life and I was encouraged by the Bible verse Philippians 4:13, “I can do all this through Him who gives me strength.” With no second thought or even doubt, I gave my name to learn and operate the mixer.

Today, I thank and praise God for enabling me to operate the 16 channel mixer in my church, and that too I am the only female sound operating technician in the crew. I strongly believe that this is one of the greatest talents I have been gifted by God to use for His kingdom.
Shouted at from the stage
5Talents: What important lessons has the Lord taught you through your talent?

As I was operating the mixer in a Sunday service during the praise and worship session, there was a minor mistake while operating the mixer. Soon, one of the senior members of the crew yelled at me directly from the stage, without even noticing about the people around. I felt so bad and hurt inside and was disappointed by the act. I left the place immediately and didn't talk to the person for almost a week.

The next day when I was meditating on His word in my quiet time, God spoke to me through the scripture portion I was reading, Matthew 23:12: “For whoever exalts himself will be humbled and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.” The lesson I was taught by the Lord from that situation was to be patient, humble, and to have a willing heart to listen to the corrections when something goes wrong in life.
5Talents: What would you say to someone who says, “I am not very talented; how could God use me?”

My dear friends, I would like you to go through the Bible verse Jeremiah 1:5, which says, “Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, before you were born, I set you apart…” This clearly states that God has planted a seed of talent in every individual before we could be born on this earth, and has made us apart to be a unique piece to be used for His kingdom.

I encourage you my friend to be patient enough to know His will and to discover the talent He has planted in you. The only thing you and I need to do is to submit ourselves to Him, trust Him completely, and He will use us for His glory. Amen!

articles.title: She walked into Newgate against advice, and found three hundred women sleeping on stone
articles.deck: Elizabeth Fry was a banker's wife with eleven children who became the first woman to give evidence to a committee of the House of Commons. What she did to English prisons, and what it cost her family.

archiveMeta.editNote: Replaces the 2013 version, which was written at primary-school reading level and could not be verified as our own work. Researched from published biography and the historical record; sources at the foot.

body.v: This piece first ran in our March 2013 issue in a much shorter form. It has been researched and written again. Sources are listed at the end.
The governor of Newgate told her not to go in. He said the women were dangerous and that he would not be responsible for what happened to her.

She went in. Inside were around three hundred women and their children in two wards, sleeping on stone with no bedding, cooking and washing and sleeping in the same space, many of them not yet tried for anything. She took off her watch first, so that nobody would be tempted.
She was a banker's wife from Norwich with a houseful of children, and she came back the next day.
Purple boots with scarlet laces

Elizabeth Gurney was born on 21 May 1780 into a wealthy Quaker family in Norwich; her father was a partner in Gurney's bank. It was money, but it was money attached to an unusually strong sense that you were answerable for what you did with it.

As a girl she found Quaker meetings dull and said so. She liked clothes, and she is remembered by her family for a pair of purple boots with scarlet laces, which is not the standard costume of a Quaker teenager. She was not obviously heading anywhere serious.

In 1798, at eighteen, she heard an American Quaker named William Savery preach in Norwich, and something in it caught. She began visiting the poor, collecting clothes, and running a small school for local children in her own home. Two years later she married Joseph Fry, a tea merchant and banker, moved to London, and over the next twenty-two years had eleven children.
For thirteen years she was, from the outside, an ordinary well-off Quaker wife with a very large family.
In 1813 a family friend came back from Newgate and described what he had seen: women and their babies on bare floors, no clothes, no doctor. She collected clothing, and went.
What she did afterwards is the part worth studying, because it was not charity. It was organisation.

In 1817 she founded the Association for the Improvement of the Female Prisoners in Newgate. It set up a school inside the prison for the children, and then for the younger women. It appointed a matron. It brought in paid needlework so the women earned something. And it drew up a set of rules — which the women themselves discussed and voted on.

That last detail is the whole method. She treated women whom the law had written off as capable of running their own affairs, and it worked well enough that officials came to look at it, and then to copy it.
The first woman to give evidence
In 1818 she was called before a committee of the House of Commons to give evidence on the state of the prisons. She was the first woman to do it.

She kept at it for decades: travelling the country and then Europe inspecting prisons, writing, and pressing officials. Her work fed directly into the reforms of the 1820s, including the Gaols Act of 1823, which required prisons to be inspected, women prisoners to be supervised by women, and gaolers to be paid rather than living off fees extracted from the inmates.

She also went to the convict ships. Women were transported to Australia for very small thefts, and were loaded aboard in irons. She got the irons stopped, and made sure each woman went with a bag of useful things: needles, thread, and cut patchwork pieces. The point was not sentiment. A woman arriving in New South Wales with a finished quilt had something to sell and a demonstrable skill, which is the difference between starting again and stealing again. One of those quilts, made aboard the ship Rajah in 1841, survives in Canberra.

She started a night shelter in London after seeing the body of a boy who had died in the street. She organised libraries for coastguard stations. And in 1840 she opened a training school for nurses — whose nurses Florence Nightingale later took with her to the Crimea.
What it cost

In 1828 her husband's bank failed. The family were ruined, Joseph was declared bankrupt, and the Society of Friends disowned him over it. Her brother had to step in. For a woman whose public standing rested partly on being unimpeachable, this was a humiliation carried out in public, and it curtailed her work for a period.

There was criticism of a more personal kind too, and it should be recorded rather than waved away. She was a mother of eleven who spent a great deal of time away from her own household doing this, and some of her children felt it. Several of them left the Quakers. Whether that is a charge or simply the arithmetic of one life is for the reader, but the arithmetic is real.
And she had public opponents. Members of Parliament argued that she was making prison comfortable and destroying its power to deter. That argument has not gone away in two hundred years.
Why she is still known
She died at Ramsgate on 12 October 1845. She had become, by some accounts, the best-known woman in England after the Queen. Between 2002 and 2017 her face was on the Bank of England five-pound note.

The system she argued for — that prisons should be inspected, that women should be supervised by women, that a prisoner is a person rather than a thing to be stored — is now so ordinary in Britain that nobody thinks of it as anyone's idea.
So what, in 2026?
The interesting thing about her is not that she was kind. Plenty of people were kind to prisoners and changed nothing at all.

What she did was build an organisation, put a matron in place, set up a school, arrange paid work, hand the women a vote on their own rules, then take the evidence to Parliament and repeat it for thirty years. She turned a feeling into a structure, and the structure outlived her by two centuries.

That is the harder half, and it is the half that usually gets left out of the story. If something makes you angry, the useful question is not how strongly you feel about it. It is what you would actually build, who would run it when you are not there, and whether you are willing to spend thirty years saying the same thing to people who are not listening yet.

Sources: Elizabeth Fry, Memoir of the Life of Elizabeth Fry, edited by two of her daughters (1847); Elizabeth Fry, Observations on the Visiting, Superintendence and Government of Female Prisoners (1827); the records of the Religious Society of Friends in Britain; the London Museum and the National Gallery of Australia on the Rajah Quilt; and the text of the Gaol Act 1823.
